Yes, NYU can take disciplinary action for conduct occurring outside the University context, but there are specific conditions under which this may happen:

The general rule is that NYU will not use its powers to interfere with the rights of a student beyond the University environment. Conduct that occurs off-campus, online, over social media, or outside the context of a University program or activity is usually subject only to the consequences of the relevant legal authority and/or public opinion.

However, the University may take disciplinary action for conduct outside the University context if that conduct "substantially disrupts the regular operation of the University or threatens the health, safety, or security of one or more members of the University community." In circumstances where conduct violates both University policy and public law, a student may be subject to both University disciplinary procedures and public sanctions [1].

In summary: NYU will generally not address conduct outside the University setting unless it substantially disrupts University operations or threatens members of the NYU community in terms of health, safety, or security [1].

Yes, the actual course plan can vary based on when courses are offered. The four-semester plan is presented as a guide to help students plan their coursework, and adjustments may be needed according to course availability or other factors [1].

**1. What semester workload does the admissions FAQ suggest for full-time employees?**

The admissions FAQ suggests that students with a full-time job should take 6 or fewer credits per semester. The full-time program is 9 credits per semester (about 40 hours of work per week, which is not recommended for those working full-time). It is advised to take a lighter load if you work full-time [1].

**2. Are evening classes guaranteed?**

No, evening classes are not guaranteed. The program tries to schedule required courses in the evenings, but this is not guaranteed. Full-time working students should have the flexibility to take required courses during the daytime if needed. Elective courses are offered both during the day and in the evenings [1].

**3. Does continuous enrollment also apply in summer?**

No, continuous enrollment is only required for fall and spring semesters. This requirement does not apply to the summer semester [2].

The Industry Concentration in the Master’s in Data Science program requires specific additional coursework and practical experience:

**Coursework:**
- Students must take two electives within the Big Data or Natural Language Processing (NLP) subject areas (6 credits). These electives are chosen from a curated list approved annually by the curriculum committee.
    - Example Big Data courses: Large Language Models: Evaluation and Applications, Database Systems, Principles of Database Systems, Information Visualization, Large-Scale Visual Analytics, Advanced Database Systems, Realtime and Big Data Analytics, Big Data Application Development, Cloud and Machine Learning, Introduction to Deep Learning and LLM-based Generative AI Systems, Database Management & Modeling, Trends in Financial Data Science, Robo Advisors & Systematic Trading.
    - Example NLP courses: Inference and Representation, Deep Learning, Fundamentals of Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models: Evaluation and Applications, Text as Data, Natural Language Processing, Learning with Large Language and Vision Models, Statistical NLP [1][2].

**Practical Experience:**
- Students are required to complete DS-GA 1009: Practical Training for Data Science, which is a 3-credit course to be taken within the first year of the program.
- This Practical Training includes a mandatory internship during the first year. International students are directed to consult NYU’s Office of Global Services regarding early CPT status if needed for an internship [1][2][3].

**Summary:**  
The Industry Concentration mandates both targeted coursework (two subject-area electives) and a substantial practical component (practical training and internship within the first year) in addition to the standard degree requirements [1][2][3].

Applicants must have completed, or have the equivalent of, the following subjects:

- Introduction to Computer Science (or a “CS-101” style programming course)
- One of the following: Calculus II, Probability, Statistics, or an advanced course in physics, engineering, or econometrics that is mathematically intensive

Preference is given to applicants with prior exposure to subjects such as machine learning, computational statistics, data mining, large-scale scientific computing, or operations research, as well as those with more advanced mathematical or computer science training than the minimum requirements. Part 2: Programming Background Expected

Applicants are expected to have had academic and/or professional experience with programming, specifically with Python and/or R at a minimum, but there are no set requirements regarding specific programming languages. The basic expectation is demonstrated familiarity with modern programming through a foundational course or equivalent experience [1].

No additional information regarding programming background or prerequisite subjects is provided in the other sources [2][3].
